title: The Cry of a Convicted Sinner

sections.heading: Coming to you as the holy King who holds my life
sections.text: Righteous and holy God, my life is in your hands, and every path I take is before you. Please do not let me drift around spiritual things like they are a hobby or a passing mood. I am unstable. My promises can disappear like smoke. I say I want to follow you, but I do not honor you as I should, and I do not live in line with your will. Make me steady. Settle me deeply in you.
theological_themes: God is holy and sovereign over the whole life of the sinner.
The sinner confesses instability, superficial religion, and failure to glorify God.
True faith needs God's preserving and stabilizing grace.

scripture_references.connection: This passage holds together human planning and God's sovereign direction of a person's steps, matching the prayer's confession that all one's ways are in God's hand.
James describes the instability of a double-minded person, which illuminates the prayer's plea to be kept from wavering and made firm before God.

sections.heading: Asking for patience while my repentance is still unfinished
sections.text: Please do not cut me off while my thoughts are still only beginning to turn into real obedience. Do not give me up while the first signs of life in me are still small and fragile. You have been far more patient with me than I deserve. You are good, slow to anger, and kind.
theological_themes: God's patience gives space for repentance and growth.
Spiritual life may begin weakly, but God can bring it to maturity.
The sinner appeals not to merit, but to God's forbearance and goodness.

scripture_references.connection: Peter explains God's patience as mercy that gives room for repentance, which directly supports the plea not to be cut off while repentance is still forming.
The image of God not crushing what is bruised or snuffing out what is faintly burning helps ground the prayer's appeal for mercy toward small, fragile beginnings of grace.

sections.heading: Rescuing me from myself and from sin's lies
sections.text: Save me from myself. Save me from the tricks and lies of sin, from the betrayal of my own crooked heart, from arguing against your verdict when you name my sin for what it is. Keep me from living as if rebellion were normal. Clear away the wrong motives, false beliefs, and selfish goals that have been driving me. I can see that my thoughts, loves, wants, and pursuits have been turned away from you.
theological_themes: Sin deceives, and the human heart is not safe as its own guide.
Conviction includes agreeing with God's judgment about sin instead of denying it.
Repentance reaches motives, desires, and aims, not only outward actions.

scripture_references.connection: Jeremiah exposes the deep deceitfulness of the human heart and God's searching judgment, which supports the prayer's request to be rescued from self-deception and perverse desires.
This passage warns believers about the deceitfulness of sin and the danger of a heart turning away from God, fitting the prayer's concern over rebellion becoming settled and normal.
The psalm asks God to search the heart and expose grievous ways, providing a biblical pattern for inviting God's judgment rather than denying his charge.

sections.heading: Confessing how serious my rebellion has been
sections.text: I have lived as though I hated you, even though you are love itself. I have pushed against your patience again and again, as if I could test how far mercy can stretch. My words and my actions have been evil. If I were a king dealing with a rebel like me, I would have crushed him long ago. If I were a father facing a child who treated me this way, I would have wanted to send him away. I have no excuse. I deserve judgment, not welcome.
theological_themes: Sin is personal rebellion against the God who is love.
God's patience is not permission to keep sinning.
Honest confession recognizes the justice of God's judgment.

scripture_references.connection: Paul warns that God's kindness and patience are meant to lead to repentance, not to be despised by continued hardness of heart; this fits the confession of having tested God's patience.
David's confession recognizes sin as ultimately against God and acknowledges God's justice in judging it, which mirrors the prayer's refusal to excuse rebellion.

sections.heading: Begging my Father and King for severe mercy
sections.text: Father of my spirit, King over my life, please do not throw me away. Do not drive me from your presence. Do whatever mercy must do in me. Pierce my heart so it can be healed. Break the hard places in me so your own hands can make me whole.
theological_themes: The sinner appeals to God as both Father and King.
True mercy may include painful conviction that leads to healing.
The deepest need is not merely relief from guilt, but restoration to God's presence and wholeness by God's hand.

scripture_references.connection: David asks God for a clean heart and pleads not to be cast away from his presence, closely matching this section's cry for inner renewal and continued access to God.
Hosea uses the language of God wounding and healing to describe repentance and restoration, supporting the prayer's request for painful but saving mercy.
Hebrews presents God's fatherly discipline as painful yet purposeful, producing holiness; this helps frame the prayer's request to be broken and healed by God's own hand.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_title: The Cry of a Convicted Sinner
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original's language about God being tempted or having his patience worn out is anthropomorphic; in the adaptation it is rendered as the sinner's arrogant testing of divine patience, not as a claim that God is weak or changeable.

The comparison to a prince crushing a rebel and a father rejecting a child is intentionally severe. It reflects the sinner's sense of deserved judgment, but could sound harsh or culturally bound if read as endorsing human cruelty or parental rejection. The adaptation preserves the force while clarifying that it is a confession of deserved judgment, not a model for human parenting.
The request that God wound and break the heart is spiritual language for conviction, contrition, and healing discipline, not a desire for self-harm or physical suffering.

The prayer assumes a strong doctrine of human sinfulness and alienation from God, in keeping with its Puritan/Reformed background. Some Christian traditions may nuance the condition of the will and affections differently.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted 'fluttering about religion' as shallow, unstable engagement with spiritual things rather than as intellectual doubt alone.
I rendered 'my thoughts grow to responses, and the budding of my soul into full flower' as early repentance and spiritual life that have not yet matured into obedience.
I treated 'denying thy charge against my offences' as resisting God's verdict about sin, so the modern prayer asks to stop arguing with God when he names sin truthfully.

I kept the concrete images of smoke, rebellion, a king, a father, wounding, breaking, and healing, but recast them in contemporary speech to avoid archaic phrasing while preserving the original's severity and hope.
